title: He Left a $200,000 Microsoft Job for an AI Startup. Revenue So Far: $6,000.
excerpt: Seattle-based Junead Khan traded a ₹1.9 crore Microsoft package for Treasury, an AI money coach — living on savings, building solo with AI tools, and documenting every failed launch.
body:
• Junead Khan, 25, walked away from a Microsoft job that paid him more than $200,000 (about ₹1.9 crore) in 2024, including stock and bonuses, to build his AI startup Treasury full-time.
  • Treasury, an AI-powered money coach born from his own struggle managing finances across the UK and the US, has generated more than $6,000 (about ₹5.4 lakh) in revenue so far.
  • Khan draws no salary and lives on his Microsoft savings — and he timed his resignation for August 2025, after stock vested and his sign-on bonus repayment window closed.
  • He credits AI coding tools like Claude Code and Codex for letting him build solo, with no co-founder and no venture capital — an approach he documents for around 30,000 social media followers.

Junead Khan had a six-figure salary, stock bonuses and a front-row seat to the artificial intelligence boom. After about two years at Microsoft, the 25-year-old walked away from that financial security to build his own AI startup — a company that, so far, has brought in a little over $6,000.

Khan, now based in Seattle, earned more than $200,000 (about ₹1.9 crore) in 2024, including stocks and bonuses, according to India Today, which reported the story from his Business Insider as-told-to account. His startup, Treasury, has generated more than $6,000 (about ₹5.4 lakh) in revenue to date — but he is not drawing a salary from the business and continues to live on the savings he accumulated at Microsoft.

Context & Background

Khan joined Microsoft full-time in 2023 after graduating in computer science from the University of North Carolina. He had been born and raised in the UK before moving to the US in 2019 for college, and his Microsoft work involved supporting the rollout of data centres around the world — valuable experience during a period of rapid AI growth.

Over time, he felt the job was not helping him learn the AI skills he wanted. After service outages in early 2025 brought a heavier emphasis on security and service stability, he felt product development slowing. Meanwhile, AI coding tools were improving fast, and he began wondering whether he could build a product on his own. He had already been working on Treasury alongside his full-time job for nearly two years — it started as an answer to his own college-era problem of managing money across two countries: an AI-powered money coach for ordinary people who can't afford a financial adviser charging thousands of dollars.

Impact & Analysis

What distinguishes Khan's leap is how deliberately he staged it. He applied to startup accelerators, including Y Combinator, hoping acceptance would give him the confidence to quit. When he wasn't selected, he reframed his Microsoft earnings as his own seed funding — and waited. He resigned only in August 2025, after some of his stock had vested and he had been at the company long enough not to repay part of his sign-on bonus. He officially launched Treasury two months later.

He also credits AI coding tools — including Claude Code and Codex — with making the solo path viable. In his telling, the tools lowered the cost of building and testing software enough that he could go without a co-founder or outside funding, a claim he road-tests publicly: he has been sharing the unvarnished journey on social media, failed launches included, and has built an audience of around 30,000 followers. Treasury now has paying customers, though Khan acknowledges the business is still early-stage — his priority is more users and more revenue before deciding whether to raise outside money.

"I didn't want to wait for somebody else to give me permission to go all in on my startup."

— Junead Khan, founder, Treasury

Diaspora Angle

Khan's story is the diaspora dream-in-reverse: a well-paid tech job at a US giant, walked away from, on purpose. His playbook is bluntly practical for anyone weighing a similar jump — treat big-tech earnings as seed funding, time the exit around vesting cliffs and bonus repayment windows, and let AI tooling replace the co-founder you can't find. If you're an Indian professional on a US work visa, note the one variable Khan didn't have to manage: his immigration status was never part of the story, and for visa-holders, a startup exit carries legal consequences an H-1B holder can't skip over — talk to an immigration attorney before resigning, because the visa is tied to the employer, not to you.

What's Next

The question now is whether Treasury can grow past its first $6,000. Khan is focused on attracting users before deciding on fundraising — the next chapter will show whether a solo-built AI product can scale without the accelerator networks and venture backing most founders lean on.

Sources: India Today, Business Insider (via MachineBrief)
